CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT NO. 2023-04
Steve Rawlings (“Applicant”) on behalf of Jacksons Food Stores, Inc.; a request to permit
the off-site sale and consumption of alcohol (Type 21- off-sale of beer, wine, and distilled
spirits) within an existing 1,400 square feet (Jacksons Food Market) convenience store
on a 0.6-acre site. The subject property is generally known as 10710 Alondra Boulevard,
located on the southeast corner of Alondra Boulevard and Piuma Avenue (also known as
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 2
Minutes of the Special Meeting  January 24, 2024

Assessor’s Parcel Number (“APN”) 7016-001-037), in the Light Manufacturing (M-1)
zone. The project includes a request for:
(1) Conditional Use Permit No. 2023-04: To permit the off-site sale and consumption of
  alcohol (Type 21- off-sale of beer, wine, and distilled spirits) within an existing 1,400
  square feet (Jacksons Food Market) convenience store; and
(2) Environmental: Consider and find that the project is exempt from the California
  Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines pursuant to Section 15301 (Existing
  Facilities).

Chair Lopez opened the public hearing.

Staff presented the legal requisites for notice of hearing. Planning Intern Estrada
presented a report stating that the request is to permit the off-site sale and consumption
of alcohol within an existing 1,400 square foot convenience store known as Jacksons
Food Market; that the convenience currently operates with a Type 20, (beer and wine),
license; that a Shell service station and car wash are also located at the site; that the
hours of operation are from 5:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m. daily with approximately two to four
employees; that the sale of alcohol will be ancillary to the existing use; that the Conditions
of Approval include the hours of alcohol sales which are from 6:00 a.m. to thirty minutes
before closing (10:30 p.m.); that the conditions require a surveillance camera system,
responsible beverage servers, and ABC licensee training for employees; that, in addition,
the sale of individual bottles or cans of distilled spirits containing less than 750 ml. is not
allowed; and that staff recommends approval of the project.

Further, Planning Intern Estrada shared that the applicant has some concerns regarding
Condition Nos. 9(f) and 9(i) which make reference to not allowing the sale of individual
bottles or cans of distilled spirits containing less than 750 ml., and that beer (including
malt liquor) cannot be sold in packages containing less than six bottles or cans as
packaged by the manufacturer or distributor, and that wine coolers cannot be sold in
packages containing less than four bottles or cans as packaged by the manufacturer or
distributor.

In response to Vice Chair Apodaca’s question if there are other convenience stores of
this size in the City that sell hard liquor, Director of Community Development Ramirez
replied that this request would be comparable to a liquor store.

Commissioner Navas commented on miniature bottles, and he asked if it is correct that
those are not allowed. Director Ramirez answered in the affirmative. Development
Services Manager Arabe added that the applicant has identified a concern with this
condition, and that the applicant has provided a packet to the Commission, prior to the
meeting, which includes proposed revisions to this condition as well as to Condition 9(i).
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 3
Minutes of the Special Meeting  January 24, 2024

The applicant’s representative, Steve Rawlings, stated that they concur with staff’s
recommendation, but that they were hoping that consideration be given to modifying two
of the conditions. Further, Mr. Rawlings commented on Jacksons Food Stores indicating
that the packet he provided to the Commission includes background information on
Jacksons Food Stores; that they are one of the largest operators of gas stations and
convenience stores in the Western United States, based out of Idaho; that they are fairly
new to California; that they made an acquisition of a company that owned thirty plus
stations, including the subject site; that they would like to be able to offer their customers
the opportunity to purchase distilled spirits, especially “Truly’s” which are malt-based
types of beverages that require a Type 21 license; that they are not trying to be a liquor
store; that the bottles would be kept behind the cashier; that they are dedicating about
four coolers to the display of beer, wine and malt liquor; that in working with Public Safety,
they seemed to be supportive of it, but that they were a little bit reluctant to allow them to
continue to allow single cans of beer; that, right now, in their other stores customers can
buy a single 16 oz. can of “Modelo”; that staff shared that if they have the privilege of
adding distilled spirits that they not be allowed to sell in quantities less than a six-pack;
that, however, Public Safety indicated that they might be amenable to changing the
condition to a three-pack; that their preference would be to continue to be able to sell
“Modelo’s” as a single; and that they are not interested in selling the big 40 oz. malt liquor
Schlitz Colt 45s.

Mr. Rawlings stated that their proposed revision is to allow them to sell singles less than
24-oz. Further, he shared that Jacksons Food Stores is a responsible company; that they
have not encountered any issues with their operation; that they do understand that every
community has their own standards; that they hope to get a little flexibility in the conditions
to be able to inventory some of their ready-to-serve beverages in the cooler; that they
would like to continue to be able to sell beer and malt beverages as a single; that he
believes that Public Safety would be willing to allow them to sell pre-packaged three-
packs; that all of their employees go through extensive training; and that he appreciated
working with City staff.

A resident on Molette Street commented on the applicant’s request. She stated that their
request is outside of what is usually granted to stores such as this; and that her main
concern is what will stop the other convenience stores from requesting the same privilege.

Director Ramirez stated that a Conditional Use Permit is to actively be engaged with the
operators on how they manage their product on a regular basis; that the subject permit
request is very restrictive and very specific; that Public Safety and Code Enforcement will
be able to enforce and monitor how they will be operating; that this gives the City more
certainty in ensuring that they will be operating in a manner consistent with their approval;
that with a Conditional Use Permit process, this is based on location; that the activity and
action that the Commission might take tonight doesn’t necessarily translate into
automatically allowing other similar uses the same privilege; that a Conditional Use Permit
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 4
Minutes of the Special Meeting  January 24, 2024

is site specific and unique to that site, and that the conditions are tailored for that particular
location; that if another similar facility came in and asked for the same request, staff would
have to make findings specific to that site, such as the individual operation, the location,
the surrounding properties and the nature of calls for service, as well as the compatibility
with the land uses in that area.

In response to Chair Lopez’ question of the applicant’s representative, if he wished to
make a rebuttal statement, Mr. Rawlings thanked the resident for her comments. Further,
he indicated that, as stated by the Director, such requests are considered on a case-by-
case basis as many factors come into play; that obtaining a Type 21 license allows them
the ability to inventory the distilled products; that he has emphasized that their track record
in all of their other stores shows that they are not interested in becoming a liquor store;
that with any Conditional Use Permit they can limit the display area that an applicant can
utilize for the display of alcoholic beverages; that, in their case, they indicated on their
plans that they want eight (8) square feet of the area behind the cashiers and four (4)
coolers; and that they might ask for a fifth cooler.

Public Safety Director, Ozzie Ramos, addressed the Planning Commission. He stated
that his primary responsibility is to keep the City safe; that in making their decision, he
would like to provide the Commission with some contexts about why the single sales
should be prohibited in the City of Norwalk; that with him tonight is the neighborhood
prosecutor that the City works with, Mr. Jim Eckart, who in 2022, was intimately involved
in addressing some of the nuisances they had in the community; and why it is important
to look at these Conditional Use Permits.

Mr. Eckart stated that, as the Commission knows, when a business comes in and applies
for a Conditional Use Permit or does a modification, the City wants to do an initial
evaluation as to the type of business they are conducting and see what best suits within
the City; that they had many issues with locations that sell for off-site consumption of
liquor, whether they are liquor stores or markets; that in 2022, they addressed the issue
of Mike’s Liquor as a result not only of an amortization period with respect to its lack of a
Conditional Use Permit and the nuisances that generated around that liquor store, many
of which dealt with the alcohol sales; that they do have lots of issues with people
consuming alcohol in public, and that it is typically with people purchasing the single cans
as opposed to purchasing the larger sizes; that one of the things that they advised the
Planning Commission and the City Council in 2022 was that they would start evaluating
and coming up with some standardized conditions intended to be imposed on all new
liquor sales locations as well as on those facilities that seek modifications of their alcohol
licenses; and that, in addition, those locations that create actual nuisances will be
addressed for either suspension, modification or revocation of an alcohol sales ability.

Continuing with his presentation, Mr. Eckart shared that the cessation of allowing sales
of single bottles or cans will have a great impact on decreasing the types of nuisance
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 5
Minutes of the Special Meeting  January 24, 2024

activities experienced by the City that surround liquor stores and other stores where
alcohol is sold. Further, he commented on Mr. Rawlings’ objection to not allowing the
sale of individual bottles of distilled spirits that are of a smaller type size; that the condition
sought to be imposed would be a prohibition of the sale of individual containers of distilled
spirits that are smaller than 750 ml; that they are trying to prevent the sale of airplane-
size bottles; that Mr. Rawlings indicated that part of the concern is that Jacksons and
other businesses want to sell ready-to-serve liquors, like the “Truly’s”, that are pre-mixed
and tend to come in smaller containers; that this condition is not prohibiting the sale of
those, it is just prohibiting the sale of individualized containers; that with respect to
Condition No. 9(i), the applicant is requesting a modification to prohibit the sales of beer
in containers of greater than 24 ounces but allow the sale of singles; that this is a big
issue for the City as it creates a greater likelihood of alcohol consumption outside of those
locations; that it also creates other issues such as people urinating in public, littering and
loitering; that they are trying to create conditions that are going to prevent those types of
activities and impose those conditions across the board.

In response to Vice Chair Apodaca’s question if prepackaged cans or bottles that come
in a two-pack or three-pack would be considered a single use, Mr. Eckart indicated that
this would not be the case. He stated that the actual condition, as it reads right now, is
that they would have to sell them in packages of six or more as packaged by the
manufacturer or distributor; and that in speaking with Mr. Rawlings, he is requesting that
three-packs be allowed as packaged by the manufacturer or distributor.

Mr. Rawlings shared that they are amenable to the conditions; that perhaps they could
look at a revision to the conditions to indicate a three-pack as opposed to a six-pack; and
that if the condition allows them to sell a six-pack of “Truly’s”, then they are fine with that.

Public Safety Director Ramos stated that he realizes that the packaging is coming out
with three-packs; that, provided it is not packaged by the applicant, he is willing to approve
that provided that they have an automatic hearing within six months to determine if any
nuisance has been caused by those sales.

Director Ramirez indicated that a hearing would be scheduled six months after approval
has been issued by the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control.

Mr. Eckart stated that in speaking with Mr. Rawlings, he is in agreement with that
condition. Further, he shared that Condition No. 9(f), which refers to the sale of individual
bottles or cans of distilled spirits containing less than 750 ml. remains the same, and that
Condition No. 9(i) be revised, in part, to change the reference to six-bottles or cans to
three bottles or cans as packaged by the manufacturer or distributor.

Since there were no other persons wishing to present testimony, Chair Lopez closed the
public hearing.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 6
Minutes of the Special Meeting  January 24, 2024

Vice Chair Apodaca shared that a lot of information has been provided tonight; that she
agrees to allow the sale of three-packs as packaged by the manufacturer or distributor;
and that she is definitely against the sale of singles and the airline sizes.

Commissioner Barragan stated that she agrees with the comments made by Vice Chair
Apodaca; and that working with Public Safety will address any issues that may come up
in the future.

Commissioner Garcia indicated that he is glad that the applicant addressed the training
of the employees; and that he supports the recommendation made by Mr. Ramos.

Commissioner Navas shared that he, too, agrees with Mr. Ramos’ recommendations.

Chair Lopez thanked Mr. Ramos and Mr. Eckart for attending this meeting and for their
input. She stated that she is also in agreement with the revised conditions.

It was moved by Vice Chair Apodaca and seconded by Commissioner Navas to: (1) adopt
Resolution No. 24-01 to approve Conditional Use Permit No. 2023-04 subject to revised
conditions as follows: That Condition No. 9(h) (combined Nos. g and h) provide that beer
(including malt liquor) shall not be sold in packages containing less than three (3) bottles
or cans as packaged by the manufacturer or distributor; and wine coolers shall not be
sold in packages containing less than three (3) bottles or cans as packaged by the
manufacturer or distributor; that a new Condition No. 9(i) be added to state that within six
(6) months of the issuance of a Type 21 alcohol license, CUP No. 2023-04 shall be
reviewed by the Planning Commission for compliance with all conditions of approval; and
(2) Considered and found that the project is exempt from the California Environmental
Quality Act pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15301 (Existing Facilities).

ON ROLL CALL VOTE
AYES: Commissioner Barragan, Commissioner Garcia, Commissioner Navas,
 Vice Chair Apodaca and Chair Lopez
NOES: None

back to Commissioner Navas on this matter. Commissioner Navas also commented on

Director of Community Development, John P. Ramirez, presented a Power Point
presentation on a project which has been in the works for several years, located on the
block between San Antonio/Firestone/Clarkdale and Front Street. He shared that there
is a vacant bank building on the southeast corner at the intersection of Firestone and San
Antonio; that at Clarkdale and Front Street there is the former Norwalk Records building;
that the City, up until earlier today, owned lots 3 and 4 shown on the Power Point
rendering; that the City also owns the parking lot across the street at Goodie’s; that
Primestor purchased the bank building about two years ago, which included lots 1 and 2
highlighted in yellow on the Power Point presentation and another lot, not highlighted,
south of lot 4; that they took a potential land swap agreement to the City Council for
consideration a couple of months ago; that, today, the agreement is being finalized; that,
effectively tomorrow, they are swapping the land with Primestor; that the City will own lots
1 and 2 and Primestor will own lots 3 and 4.

Continuing with his presentation, Director Ramirez shared that one of the goals of this
land swap is to enable Primestor to combine the other lots that they have purchased that
are located south of lots 3 and 4. Further, he stated that this is a unique opportunity for
the City and for Primestor to look at ways to revitalize the area and engage in more
community activities; that Primestor is actively recruiting businesses to locate in the
Norwalk Records store; that this location is a part of their efforts on the Heart of Norwalk,
which they will be bringing before Council next month to discuss the overall land use plan
for the Heart of Norwalk; that as this project is considered to be a part of the Heart of
Norwalk, one of the goals is to find a way to develop the site as a mixed use project and
revitalize the commercial area on Front Street as well as create an opportunity for another
project; that the exchange facilitates a 76-unit affordable workforce housing and market
rate project, revitalizes the Front Street commercial area, and furthers the targets in their
Housing Element and General Plan.

Director Ramirez shared that as part of the State’s encouragement to have housing
developed, they processed this project under a new State law called AB 2011 which went
into effect in 2022; that the goal of AB 2011 is to facilitate the development of affordable
housing and the development of jobs; that, under this new law, projects move forward in
an administrative fashion and have housing built and approved without having a public
hearing and without having to go through a public hearing process with the California
Environmental Quality Act.

Further, he commented on the land swap stating that the proposed project does not need
to go before the Planning Commission or the City Council; and that the developer is
working on the design and engineering for the construction of the project.

 INTRODUCTION

On February 29, 1996, the Norwalk City Council adopted the City's current General Plan
for implementation. The General Plan contains ten (10) elements: Land Use, Circulation,
Housing, Conservation, Open Space, Noise, Safety, Community Design, Educational and
Cultural Resources, and Utility Infrastructure. Of these elements, Community Design,
Educational and Cultural Resources and Utility Infrastructure are the three new elements
that were added to the General Plan as part of the 1996 comprehensive General Plan
update.

In February of 2023, the City Council adopted the 2021-2029 Housing Element.
Throughout 2022, the Norwalk Planning Commission worked on the implementation of
the approved Housing Element to adequately address issues related to current and future
housing opportunities and to meet the requirements of the Department of Housing and
Community Development (HCD).

As required by Government Code Section 65400(b), every city must submit an annual
progress report to their legislative body, the Governor’s Office of Planning and Research
(OPR), and the Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) on the
implementation status of their General Plan. The annual report must also include
discussion on the City's progress in providing its required share of affordable housing
pursuant to Government Code Section 65584 and its efforts to remove governmental
constraints for the maintenance, improvement and development of affordable housing per
Section 65583(c)(3) of the California Government Code.

This General Plan and Housing Element Annual Progress Report covers the period from
January 1, 2023 to December 31, 2023.

Land Use Element

The City of Norwalk is considered a developed community comprised mostly of single-
family residential neighborhoods, with its predominant commercial and industrial land
uses situated along several major roadways. As a developed community, any future
development in the City would occur as infill or redevelopment.

In February 1996, an updated Land Use Element was adopted as part of the City's
comprehensive General Plan update. Since adoption of the 1996 General Plan, the City
has processed a variety of new land use developments and adopted new land use
regulations that have continually upheld the Land Use Element.

Circulation Element

The Circulation Element of the 1996 General Plan defines the transportation needs of the
City and presents a comprehensive transportation plan to accommodate those needs.
The element also focuses on identifying and evaluating local circulation needs, while
balancing those needs with regional demands and mandates. The following outlines the
City’s efforts in addressing local circulation, regional circulation and public transportation
needs in the Norwalk community:

Local Circulation

The City has continued to make a variety of street and traffic improvements to its existing
network of public streets and sidewalks (e.g., street resurfacing, sidewalk repair,
Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) compliance, traffic signal modifications, etc.).
These street and traffic improvements are identified as Capital Improvement Projects in
which federal, state and local funding sources are utilized to execute the projects.

The City worked on the following Capital Improvement Projects to enhance local streets
and sidewalks in the 2023 calendar year:

   Continued annual construction work to repair/replace damaged curbs gutters and
  sidewalks throughout the City;

Other street improvements (e.g., street dedications, street widening, sidewalk
construction, deceleration lanes, etc.) are funded and built by developers as part of their
conditions of approval for developing their property. In addition, developers are
responsible for paying their "fair share" of the cost to mitigate anticipated traffic impacts
associated with new development in the City.

Additionally, developers are often required to conduct traffic studies to establish uses
which have higher parking demands or larger development projects which may create
traffic impacts on the existing network of public streets. These traffic studies are required
to ensure that new uses and developments will not have negative traffic impacts.

Public Transportation

In addition to conducting street and circulation improvements, the City also provides
public transportation services for the City and surrounding communities through the
Norwalk Transit System (NTS). As one of sixteen (16) municipal bus operators within Los
Angeles County, NTS was established as a municipal fixed-route operation on August 1,
1974. Later the same year, a demand-responsive service, also known as Dial-a-Ride
(DAR), was implemented to better serve the elderly and disabled in 2002, utilizing lift-
equipped accessible vans.

Fixed-Route Service: The fixed-route service utilizes thirty-four (34) buses which provide
local circulated and inter-jurisdictional service within Norwalk and the adjoining
communities of Artesia, Bellflower, Cerritos, El Monte, La Mirada, La Habra, Santa Fe
Springs, South El Monte, Whittier, and the portions of unincorporated Los Angeles
County; as well as, providing bus service as a link between the Metro Greenline Light Rail

The Conservation Element of the Norwalk General Plan is intended to provide for the
conservation, development and utilization of natural resources (e.g., water, minerals,
energy sources etc.). Since the City of Norwalk is a completely urbanized community,
there are limited natural resources that can be conserved and/or developed. However,
conservation of existing resources from contamination and providing adequate mitigation
measures to ensure that new development does not adversely impact the existing
environment is being routinely achieved. The following is a discussion of different City
conservation efforts as they relate to water conservancy and recycling programs:

Water
In the on-going effort to improve water quality and eliminate pollutant discharges into
municipal storm drains and underground aquifers, the Engineering Division is currently
responsible for City compliance with the federally mandated National Pollutant Discharge
Elimination System (NPDES). As part of this program, an annual stormwater report is
submitted to the Regional Water Quality Control Board as required by the NPDES permit.

Further, the City is working to capture and treat stormwater through implementation of its
Low Impact Development Program (LID) and incorporation of LID Best Management
Practices (BMPs) in Capital Improvement Projects (CIP) projects.

Recycling
The City of Norwalk is committed to “going green,” promoting public awareness on the
importance of recycling/conservation and offering programs for its residents. All of the
City’s recycling programs are funded either by grants, partnerships, and/or forfeiture
funds. Below is a summary of the various recycling programs and outreach efforts that
took place in the 2023 calendar year within the City.

  Used Oil Block Grants/Oil Payment Program – This program is funded by
  CalRecycle. In the 2023 calendar year, the funds were used to fund year-round
  residential curbside pickups. In 2023, four (4) filter exchange events were held, at
  which residents were able to take their used motor oil and filters to a certified
  collection center to exchange for a brand new, free filter. Promotional items such
  as oil containers, funnels, cardboard “creepers,” and cleaning rags were also
  distributed during these events.

  Energy Efficiency Conservation – During the 2023 calendar year, the City’s energy
  conservation efforts were focused to online and print messaging to reach the
  public. When possible, energy conservation messaging was spread via social
  media.

  City E-waste and Shredding Events – The City organized one electronic waste
  collection and document shredding event in February 2023. The event was held
  on a Saturday from 9 a.m. - 2 p.m. in the City Hall parking lot. Through this event,
  ten (10) tons of electronic waste was diverted from the waste stream along with
  nine (9) tons of paper that were securely shredded and reused.

  Construction and Demolition (C&D) Recycling – In response to AB 939 (codified in
  Public Resources Code § 41780), the mandatory recycling requirement to divert
  at least 50% of discarded materials from landfills, the City requires property
  owners/contractors to submit a Waste Management Plan (WMP) along with a fully
  refundable deposit for construction and demolition projects. Those that fail to
  comply with submitting disposal and recycling receipts will have their deposits
  forfeited. The forfeiture funds are then used to fund City recycling efforts.

  Public Education – The City contracts with Eco Partners to prepare and print “One
  Person’s Trash,” a quarterly publication exclusively devoted to recycling and
  conservation topics. The publication is funded by the City’s trash hauler, Athens
  Services.

  Mandatory Commercial Recycling – To achieve the goals of Public Resources
  Code §41780.02, the City has partnered with the City’s authorized waste hauler to
  disseminate information about the mandatory commercial recycling requirement
  for businesses and apartment complexes with five (5) or more units. Information
  was disseminated through direct mailings as well as in City publications. The City
  is already in compliance with the law, since waste collected from businesses and
  apartment complexes in Norwalk go through a sorting process where recyclables
  are removed from the waste stream. However, the City encourages businesses
  and apartment complexes to look into additional recycling options when feasible.

Community Design Element

Although the Community Design Element does not prescribe a set of particular design

Development Review and Approval
Prior to the construction of any new or remodeled development in the City, proposed
projects must go through a development review process in which the Community
Development Department works with developers and property owners to ensure
compliance with the City’s zoning requirements as well as aesthetic considerations such
as architectural style, scale, massing and building orientation. These are important design
features associated with any new or remodeled development, particularly, when a project
design may impact the surrounding physical environment.

The Planning Commission is the approving body for all projects that require discretionary
approval and is responsible for ensuring that projects are:

    Compatible with other developments in the area and will have a positive effect on
  the appearance of the surrounding neighborhood;
    Consistent with the General Plan;
    Will not be detrimental to the public health, safety, and welfare or adversely affect
  property values or the present or future development of surrounding areas; and
    Compliant with the regulations contained within the Norwalk Municipal Code.

The City takes into account all design considerations during the development review
process, and promotes and obtains aesthetically attractive, quality developments
throughout the City. In 2023, the Planning Commission continued to hold developers and
